contenido: 1. The consecrated life, deeply rooted in the examples and teachings of Christ the Lord, is a gift from God the Father to his Church through the Spirit. With the profession of the evangelical counsels, the characteristic features of Jesus – virgin, poor and obedient – ​​have a typical and permanent “visibility” in the middle of the world, and the gaze of the faithful is drawn to the mystery of the Kingdom of God that already acts in history, but awaits its full realization in heaven.

2. The role of consecrated life in the Church is so important that I decided to convene a Synod to deepen its meaning and perspectives, in view of the already imminent new millennium. I wanted numerous consecrated men and women to be present at the Synodal Assembly, along with the Fathers, so that their contribution to the common reflection would not be lacking.

3. The universal presence of consecrated life and the evangelical character of its testimony clearly show - if necessary - that it is not an isolated and marginal reality, but rather encompasses the entire Church. The Bishops in the Synod have confirmed it many times: "de re nostra agitur", "it is something that affects us." In reality, consecrated life is at the very heart of the Church as a decisive element for its mission, since it "indicates the intimate nature of the Christian vocation" and the aspiration of the entire Bride Church towards union with the only Bridegroom. In the Synod it has been affirmed on several occasions that consecrated life has not only played a role of help and support for the Church in the past, but is also a precious and necessary gift for the present and future of the People of God, because it belongs intimately to its life, its holiness and its mission.

4. Adhering to the desire expressed by the ordinary general assembly of the Synod of Bishops gathered to reflect on the theme "Consecrated life and its mission in the Church and in the world", I want to present in this Apostolic Exhortation the fruits of the synod itinerary, and show all the faithful "Bishops, priests, deacons, consecrated persons and lay people", as well as to all those who put themselves at the Listen, the wonders that the Lord also wants to accomplish today through consecrated life.

5. How can we not remember with gratitude to the Spirit the multitude of historical forms of consecrated life, raised by Him and still present in the ecclesial environment? These appear like a plant full of branches that sinks its roots in the Gospel and bears abundant fruit in each era of the Church. What extraordinary wealth! I myself, at the end of the Synod, felt the need to point out this constant element in the history of the Church: the numerous founders and foundresses, male and female saints, who have chosen Christ in evangelical radicalism and in fraternal service, especially to the poor and abandoned. Precisely this service clearly shows how consecrated life manifests the unitary character of the commandment of love, in the inseparable link between love of God and love of neighbor.

6. The Synod Fathers of the Eastern Catholic Churches and the representatives of the other Churches of the East have pointed out in their interventions the evangelical values of monastic life, which arose from the beginning of Christianity and is still flourishing in their territories, especially in the Orthodox Churches.

7. It is a reason for joy and hope to see how the ancient Order of virgins flourishes again today, witnessed in Christian communities since apostolic times. Consecrated by the diocesan Bishop, they assume a special bond with the Church, to whose service they dedicate themselves, even while remaining in the world. Alone or in association, they constitute a special eschatological image of the heavenly Bride and the future life, when the Church finally lives the love of Christ the husband to the full.

8. Institutes oriented completely toward contemplation, formed by women or men, are for the Church a source of glory and a source of heavenly graces. With their life and mission, their members imitate Christ praying on the mountain, testify to the lordship of God over history and anticipate future glory.

9. In the West, multiple other expressions of religious life have flourished over the centuries, in which countless people, renouncing the world, have consecrated themselves to God through the public profession of the evangelical counsels according to a specific charisma and in a stable form of common life, for a multiform apostolic service to the People of God. Thus, the various families of Regular Canons, the mendicant Orders, the Regular Clerics and, in general, the male and female religious Congregations dedicated to apostolic and missionary activity and to the multiple works that Christian charity has given rise to.

10. The Holy Spirit, admirable architect of the variety of charisms, has raised up in our time new forms of consecrated life, as if wanting to correspond, according to a providential plan, to the new needs that the Church encounters today when carrying out its mission in the world.

11. The Societies of apostolic life or common life, male and female, also deserve special mention, which seek, with their own style, a specific apostolic or missionary goal. In many of them, with sacred ties officially recognized by the Church, evangelical counsels are expressly assumed. However, even in this case the peculiarity of their consecration distinguishes them from religious Institutes and secular Institutes. The peculiarity of this way of life must be safeguarded and promoted, which in the course of recent centuries has produced so many fruits of holiness and apostolate, especially in the field of charity and in the missionary dissemination of the Gospel.

12. The perennial youth of the Church continues to manifest itself today as well: in recent decades, after the Second Vatican Ecumenical Council, new or renewed forms of consecrated life have emerged. In many cases these are Institutes similar to those already existing, but born from new spiritual and apostolic impulses. Their vitality must be discerned by the authority of the Church, which is responsible for carrying out the necessary examinations both to prove the authenticity of the purpose that has inspired them, and to avoid the excessive multiplication of institutions analogous to each other, with the consequent risk of harmful fragmentation into groups that are too small. In other cases they are original experiences, which are seeking their own identity in the Church and hope to be officially recognized by the Apostolic See, the only authority responsible for the final judgment.

13. Gathering the fruits of the synodal work, I want to address with this Apostolic Exhortation to the entire Church, to offer not only the consecrated persons, but also the Pastors and the faithful, the results of an encouraging encounter, over whose development the Holy Spirit has not ceased to watch over with his gifts of truth and love.

14. The evangelical foundation of consecrated life must be sought in the special relationship that Jesus, in his earthly life, established with some of his disciples, inviting them not only to welcome the Kingdom of God in their own lives, but to put their own existence at the service of this cause, leaving everything and closely imitating his way of life.

15. «Six days later, Jesus takes with him Peter, James, and his brother John, and leads them aside to a high mountain. And he was transfigured before them: his face became bright as the sun and his clothes became white as light. At this, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, talking with him.

16. The Father's call is addressed to the three ecstatic disciples to listen to Christ, to place all trust in Him, to make Him the center of life. In the word that comes from above, the invitation with which Jesus himself, at the beginning of public life, had called them to follow him, takes them out of their ordinary life and welcomes them into his intimacy. Precisely from this special grace of intimacy arises, in consecrated life, the possibility and requirement of total self-giving in the profession of evangelical counsels. These, rather than a renunciation, are a specific acceptance of the mystery of Christ, lived in the Church.

17. Contemplation of the glory of the Lord Jesus in the icon of the Transfiguration reveals to consecrated people first of all the Father, creator and giver of all good, who draws to himself ( [+[0]+] ) a creature of his with a special love for a special mission. «This is my beloved Son: listen to him» ([+[1]+]). Responding to this invitation accompanied by an inner attraction, the called person entrusts themselves to the love of God who wants them to be at his exclusive service, and consecrates themselves totally to Him and to His plan of salvation ( [+[2]+] ).

18. The Son, the path that leads to the Father ( [+[0]+] ), calls all those that the Father has given him ( [+[1]+] ) to a following that guides their existence. But from some – precisely consecrated people – he asks for a total commitment, which involves abandoning all things ([+[2]+]) to live in intimacy with Him and follow Him wherever He goes ([+[3]+]).
19. «A bright cloud covered them with its shadow» ([+[0]+]). A significant spiritual interpretation of the Transfiguration sees in this cloud the image of the Holy Spirit.

20. The evangelical counsels are, therefore, above all a gift from the Holy Trinity. The consecrated life is an announcement of what the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit, accomplishes with his love, his goodness and his beauty. Indeed, «the religious state [...] reveals in a special way the superiority of the Kingdom over everything created and its radical demands. "It also shows all men the extraordinary greatness of the power of Christ the King and the infinite effectiveness of the Holy Spirit, who works wonders in his Church."

21. The reference of the evangelical counsels to the holy and sanctifying Trinity reveals its deepest meaning. Indeed, they are an expression of the love of the Son for the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit. By practicing them, the consecrated person lives with particular intensity the Trinitarian and Christological character that characterizes the entire Christian life.

22. Consecrated life "imitates more closely and continually makes present in the Church", by the impulse of the Holy Spirit, the way of life that Jesus, supreme consecrated person and missionary of the Father for his Kingdom, embraced and proposed to the disciples who followed him ([+[0]+]). In the light of the consecration of Jesus, it is possible to discover in the initiative of the Father, source of all holiness, the original principle of consecrated life. Indeed, Jesus himself is the one whom God "anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power" ([+[1]+]), "the one whom the Father has sanctified and sent into the world" ([+[2]+]). Accepting the consecration of the Father, the Son in turn consecrates himself to Him for humanity ([+[3]+]): his life of virginity, obedience and poverty manifests his filial and total adherence to the Father's plan ([+[4]+]). His perfect oblation confers a meaning of consecration to all the events of his earthly existence.

23. The dazzling event of the Transfiguration prepares that other dramatic, but no less luminous, event of Calvary. Peter, James and John contemplate the Lord Jesus together with Moses and Elijah, with whom - according to the evangelist Luke - he speaks "of his departure, which he was going to accomplish in Jerusalem" ([+[0]+]). The eyes of the apostles are fixed on Jesus who thinks about the Cross ( [+[1]+] ). There her virginal love for the Father and for all men will reach its maximum expression; their poverty will reach the stripping of everything; his obedience until the surrender of life.

24. The consecrated person, in the various forms of life raised by the Spirit throughout history, experiences the truth of God-Love in a way that is all the more immediate and profound the more they place themselves under the Cross of Christ. He who in his death appears before human eyes disfigured and without beauty to the point of moving those present to cover their faces ([+[0]+]), precisely on the Cross fully manifests the beauty and power of the love of God. Saint Augustine sings it like this: «Beautiful being God, Word in God [...] It is beautiful in heaven and it is beautiful on earth; beautiful in the bosom, beautiful in the arms of his parents, beautiful in miracles, beautiful in whippings; beautiful guest to life, beautiful not worrying about death, beautiful giving life, beautiful taking it; beautiful on the cross, beautiful in the tomb and beautiful in heaven. "Hear with understanding the song, and do not let the weakness of his flesh detract from your eyes the splendor of his beauty."

25. Mission also arises from the paschal mystery, a dimension that determines all ecclesial life. She has her own specific fulfillment in consecrated life. In fact, even beyond the charisms of the Institutes dedicated to the mission ad gentes or engaged in an activity of a properly apostolic type, it can be said that the mission is inscribed in the very heart of each form of consecrated life. To the extent that the consecrated person lives a life solely given to the Father ([+[0]+]), sustained by Christ ([+[1]+]), animated by the Spirit ([+[2]+]), he effectively cooperates with the mission of the Lord Jesus ([+[3]+]), contributing in a particularly profound way to the renewal of the world.

26. Because today apostolic concerns are increasingly urgent and dedication to the things of this world risks becoming ever more absorbing, it is particularly timely to draw attention to the eschatological nature of consecrated life.

27. « Come, Lord Jesus! » ( [+[0]+] ). This waiting is the most opposite of inertia: although directed towards the future Kingdom, it is translated into work and mission, so that the Kingdom becomes present now through the establishment of the spirit of the Beatitudes, capable of also arousing in human society effective attitudes of justice, peace, solidarity and forgiveness.

28. Mary is the one who, from her immaculate conception, most perfectly reflects divine beauty. "All beautiful" is the title with which the Church invokes her. "The relationship that every believer, as a consequence of their union with Christ, maintains with the Most Holy Mary is even more accentuated in the life of consecrated persons [...] In all ( [+[0]+] ) there is the conviction that the presence of Mary has a fundamental importance both for the spiritual life of each consecrated soul, and for the consistency, unity and progress of the entire community."

29. In the Transfiguration scene, Peter speaks on behalf of the other apostles: "It is good for us to be here" ([+[0]+]). The experience of the glory of Christ, although it enraptures his mind and heart, does not isolate him, but, on the contrary, unites him more deeply to the "we" of the disciples.

30. In the tradition of the Church, religious profession is considered a unique and fruitful deepening of the baptismal consecration in that, through it, the intimate union with Christ, already inaugurated with Baptism, is developed in the gift of a configuration more fully expressed and realized, through the profession of the evangelical counsels.
31. The various forms of life in which, according to the plan of the Lord Jesus, ecclesial life is articulated present reciprocal relationships on which it is interesting to dwell.

32. In this harmonious set of gifts, each of the fundamental states of life is entrusted with the mission of manifesting, in its own category, one or another of the dimensions of the unique mystery of Christ. If lay life has the particular mission of announcing the Gospel in the midst of temporal realities, in the area of ​​ecclesial communion, those who have received Holy Orders, especially the Bishops, develop an irreplaceable ministry. They have the task of shepherding the People of God with the teaching of the Word, the administration of the Sacraments and the exercise of sacred power at the service of the ecclesial communion, which is an organic communion, ordered hierarchically.

33. The peculiar mission of consecrated life is to keep alive in the baptized the awareness of the fundamental values of the Gospel, giving "a magnificent and extraordinary testimony that without the spirit of the Beatitudes this world cannot be transformed and offered to God." In this way, consecrated life continually enlivens in the conscience of the People of God the demand to respond with the holiness of life to the love of God poured into hearts by the Holy Spirit ([+[0]+]), reflecting in conduct the sacramental consecration wrought by God in Baptism, Confirmation or Orders. In fact, we must move from the holiness communicated by the sacraments to the holiness of daily life. Consecrated life, with its very presence in the Church, is put at the service of the consecration of the life of each faithful, layman or cleric.

34. Of particular importance is the spousal meaning of consecrated life, which refers to the Church's requirement to live in full and exclusive dedication to her Spouse, from whom she receives all good. In this spousal dimension, typical of all consecrated life, it is above all the woman who sees herself singularly reflected, as if discovering the special nature of her relationship with the Lord.

35. "When the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces to the ground, filled with fear" ([+[0]+]). The synoptics highlight the fear of the disciples in the episode of the Transfiguration, with different nuances. The attractiveness of the transfigured face of Christ does not prevent them from feeling afraid before the divine Majesty that surrounds them. Whenever man experiences the glory of God he also realizes his smallness and from this arises a feeling of fear. This fear is healthy. It reminds man of divine perfection, and at the same time pushes him with an urgent call to "holiness."
36. In the following of Christ and in the love for his person there are some points about the growth of holiness in the consecrated life that deserve to be especially highlighted today.

37. Institutes are therefore invited to courageously reproduce the audacity, creativity and holiness of their founders and foundresses in response to the signs of the times that arise in today's world. This invitation is above all a call to persevere on the path of holiness through the material and spiritual difficulties that mark daily life. But it is also called to seek competence in its own work and to cultivate a dynamic fidelity to its own mission, adapting its forms, when necessary, to new situations and diverse needs, in full docility to divine inspiration and ecclesial discernment. The conviction must remain alive, therefore, that the guarantee of any renewal that seeks to be faithful to the original inspiration is in the search for ever more complete conformation with the Lord.

38. The call to holiness is welcomed and can be cultivated only in the silence of adoration before the infinite transcendence of God: «We must confess that we all need this silence loaded with adored presence: theology, to be able to fully value our own sapiential and spiritual soul; prayer, so that you never forget that seeing God means coming down from the mountain with a face so radiant that it requires you to cover it with a veil ( [+[0]+] ) [...]; commitment, to renounce locking oneself in a struggle without love and forgiveness [...]. Everyone, both believers and non-believers, needs to learn a silence that allows the Other to speak, when he wants and how he wants, and for us to understand that word. Specifically, this involves great fidelity to liturgical and personal prayer, to times dedicated to mental prayer and contemplation, to Eucharistic adoration, monthly retreats and spiritual exercises.

39. Today more than ever, a renewed commitment to holiness on the part of consecrated people is necessary to favor and sustain the effort of every Christian for perfection. "It is necessary to arouse in each faithful a true desire for holiness, a strong desire for conversion and personal renewal in a climate of ever more intense prayer and solidarity with others, especially those most in need."

40. "Jesus approached them, touched them and said, 'Stand up, do not be afraid'" ( [+[0]+] ). Like the three apostles in the episode of the Transfiguration, consecrated people know from experience that their lives are not always illuminated by that sensitive fervor that makes them exclaim: "It is good to be here" ([+[1]+]). However, it is always a life "touched" by the hand of Christ, led by his voice and sustained by his grace.

41. During his earthly life, Jesus called those whom he wanted, to have them with him and to teach them to live according to his example, for the Father and for the mission that the Father had entrusted to him ( [+[0]+] ). In this way, he inaugurated a new family of which all those who were willing to "fulfill the will of God" would be part of throughout the centuries ([+[1]+]). After the Ascension, thanks to the gift of the Spirit, a fraternal community was formed around the Apostles, united in praise of God and in a concrete experience of communion ( [+[2]+] ). The life of this community and, above all, the experience of full participation in the mystery of Christ lived by the Twelve, have been the model by which the Church has been inspired whenever it has wanted to revive the fervor of its origins and resume its path in history with renewed evangelical vigor.

42. Fraternal life, understood as a life shared in love, is an eloquent sign of ecclesial communion. It is cultivated with special care by religious Institutes and Societies of apostolic life, in which community life acquires a peculiar meaning. But the dimension of fraternal communion is not lacking either in secular Institutes or in the individual forms of consecrated life. The hermits, in the depths of their solitude, do not separate themselves from ecclesial communion, but serve it with their own specific contemplative charisma; The consecrated virgins in the world carry out their consecration in a special relationship of communion with the particular and universal Church, as do consecrated widows and widowers in a similar way.

43. In consecrated life, the role of Superiors, including local ones, has always been of great importance, both for spiritual life and for the mission. In these years of search and transformation, the need to review this position has sometimes been felt. But it is necessary to recognize that whoever exercises authority cannot abdicate his role as the first person in charge of the community, as guide of the brothers and sisters on the spiritual and apostolic path.

44. In fraternal life, care for the elderly and the sick has an important place, especially at a time like this, when in certain regions of the world the number of consecrated people already in years increases. The caring care they deserve is not based solely on a duty of charity and recognition, but also expresses the conviction that their testimony is of great help to the Church and the Institutes, and that their mission continues to be valid and meritorious, even when, for reasons of age or illness, they have been forced to leave their own activities. They certainly have a lot to give in wisdom and experience to the community, if it knows how to be close to them with attention and listening skills.

45. Fraternal life has a fundamental role in the spiritual path of consecrated people, whether for their constant renewal or for the fulfillment of their mission in the world. This is deduced from the theological motivations that underpin it, and experience itself more than confirms it. I therefore exhort consecrated men and women to cultivate it with determination, following the example of the first Christians of Jerusalem, who were assiduous in listening to the teachings of the Apostles, in common prayer, in participating in the Eucharist, and in sharing the goods of nature and grace ([+[0]+]). Above all, I exhort men and women religious and members of Societies of Apostolic Life to live unreservedly mutual love and to manifest it in the most appropriate way to the nature of the Institute itself, so that each community may be shown as a luminous sign of the new Jerusalem, "dwelling of God with men" ([+[1]+]).

46. Consecrated life is also assigned an important role in light of the doctrine on the Church-communion, proposed with such emphasis by the Second Vatican Council. Consecrated people are asked to be truly experts in communion, and to live the respective spirituality as "witnesses and architects of that "project of communion" that constitutes the summit of the history of man according to God." The sense of ecclesial communion, when developed as a spirituality of communion, promotes a way of thinking, saying and acting, which makes the Church grow in depth and extension. The life of communion «will thus be a sign for the world and an attractive force that leads to belief in Christ [...]. In this way the communion opens to the mission, becoming itself a mission. Furthermore, "communion generates communion and is essentially configured as missionary communion."

47. Consecrated persons are called to be a leaven of missionary communion in the universal Church by the very fact that the multiple charismas of the respective Institutes are granted by the Spirit for the good of the entire mystical Body, whose edification they must serve ([+[0]+]). It is significant that, in the words of the Apostle, the "most excellent way" ([+[1]+]), the greatest of all, is charity ([+[2]+]), which harmonizes all diversities and instills in all the strength of mutual support in apostolic action. The peculiar bond of communion that the various forms of consecrated life and the Societies of apostolic life have with the Successor of Peter in his ministry of unity and missionary universality tends precisely to this. The history of spirituality profusely illustrates this connection, revealing its providential function as a guarantee of both the identity of consecrated life and the missionary expansion of the Gospel. Without the contribution of so many Institutes of consecrated life and Societies of apostolic life – as the Synod Fathers have noted – the vigorous dissemination of the Gospel proclamation, the firm roots of the Church in so many regions of the world, and the Christian spring that is witnessed today in the young Churches, would be unthinkable. They have maintained firm communion with the Successors of Peter throughout the centuries, who, in turn, have found in these Institutes a ready and generous attitude to dedicate themselves to the mission, with an availability that, when necessary, has reached true heroism.

48. Consecrated persons also have a significant role within particular Churches. This is an aspect that, based on the conciliar doctrine on the Church as communion and mystery, and on the particular Churches as a portion of the People of God, in which "the one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church of Christ is truly present and acts", has been developed and regulated by several successive documents. In the light of these texts, the importance of the collaboration of consecrated persons with the Bishops for the harmonious development of diocesan pastoral care appears clearly. The charismas of consecrated life can contribute powerfully to the building of charity in the particular Church.

49. The Bishop is father and pastor of the entire particular Church. It is his responsibility to recognize and respect each of the charisms, promote them and coordinate them. In his pastoral charity he must welcome, therefore, the charism of consecrated life as a grace that does not concern only one Institute, but that concerns and benefits the entire Church. It will seek, therefore, to support and provide help to consecrated people, so that, in communion with the Church and faithful to the founding inspiration, they open themselves to spiritual and pastoral perspectives in harmony with the demands of our time. Consecrated persons, for their part, will not fail to offer their generous collaboration to the particular Church according to their own strength and respecting their own charism, acting in full communion with the Bishop in the field of evangelization, catechesis and the life of the parishes.

50. To promote reciprocal knowledge, which is an obligatory requirement for effective cooperation, especially in the pastoral field, a constant dialogue between the Superiors of the Institutes of consecrated life and Societies of apostolic life with the Bishops is always appropriate. Thanks to these regular contacts, the Superiors will be able to inform the Bishops about the apostolic initiatives they wish to undertake in their dioceses, to reach the necessary operational agreements with them. In the same way, it is appropriate that delegates of the Conferences of Major Superiors be invited to attend the assemblies of the Conferences of Bishops, and that, vice versa, delegates of the Episcopal Conferences be invited to the Conferences of Superiors, according to the modalities that are determined. In this perspective, it will be very useful if, where they do not yet exist, mixed commissions of Bishops and Major Superiors are established and operational at the national level, which together examine problems of common interest. The insertion of the theology and spirituality of consecrated life in the theological study plan of diocesan priests will also contribute to a better mutual knowledge, as well as the provision in the formation of consecrated persons of an adequate study of the theology of the particular Church and the spirituality of the diocesan clergy.

51. The Church entrusts to communities of consecrated life the particular task of fostering the spirituality of communion, first of all within itself and, furthermore, in the ecclesial community itself and even beyond its confines, constantly establishing or reestablishing the dialogue of charity, especially where today's world is torn by ethnic hatred or homicidal madness. Located in the diverse societies of our world - frequently torn by conflicting passions and interests, desirous of unity but undecided about the path to follow - communities of consecrated life, in which people of different ages, languages ​​and cultures live together as brothers and sisters, are presented as a sign of an always possible dialogue and a communion capable of bringing diversities into harmony.

52. The ecclesial sense of communion also nourishes and sustains the fraternal spiritual relationship and mutual collaboration between the various Institutes of consecrated life and Societies of apostolic life. People who are united among themselves by the common commitment to follow Christ and animated by the same Spirit, cannot fail to make visible, like branches of a single Vine, the fullness of the Gospel of love. Always remaining faithful to their own charism, but keeping in mind the spiritual friendship that has frequently united various founders and foundresses on earth, these people are called to manifest an exemplary fraternity, which serves as a stimulus to the other ecclesial components in the daily commitment to bear witness to the Gospel.

53. The Conferences of Superiors and Major Superiors and the Conferences of Secular Institutes can make a notable contribution to communion. Stimulated and regulated by the Second Vatican Council and subsequent documents, these organizations have as their main objective the promotion of consecrated life, embedded in the fabric of the ecclesial mission.

54. One of the fruits of the doctrine of the Church as a communion in recent years has been the awareness that its various members can and must join forces, in an attitude of collaboration and exchange of gifts, in order to participate more effectively in the ecclesial mission. In this way, it contributes to presenting a more articulated and complete image of the Church, while at the same time it is easier to provide answers to the great challenges of our time with the choral contribution of the different gifts.

55. These new paths of communion and collaboration deserve to be encouraged for various reasons. Indeed, from this it will be possible to derive above all an active irradiation of spirituality beyond the borders of the Institute, which will have new energies, thus ensuring the Church the continuity of some of its most typical forms of service. Another positive consequence may also consist of joining efforts between consecrated people and lay people in order to the mission: moved by the example of holiness of consecrated people, the lay people will be introduced to the direct experience of the spirit of the evangelical counsels and encouraged to live and witness to the spirit of the Beatitudes to transform the world according to the heart of God.

56. A significant manifestation of lay participation in the richness of consecrated life is the adhesion of lay faithful to the various Institutes under the formula of the so-called associate members or, according to the demands of some cultural environments, of people who share, for a certain time, the community life and the particular dedication to contemplation or the apostolate of the Institute, provided, obviously, that the identity of the Institute in its internal life does not suffer any damage.

57. The Church fully reveals its multiform spiritual wealth when, overcoming all discrimination, it welcomes as an authentic blessing the gifts poured out by God on both men and women, estimating them in their equal dignity. Consecrated women are called to be in a very special way, and through their dedication lived fully and with joy, a sign of God's tenderness towards the human race and a singular testimony of the mystery of the Church, which is virgin, wife and mother. This mission was evident in the Synod, in which several of them participated and in which they had the opportunity to make their voices heard and appreciated by all. Thanks to their contributions, some useful indications have emerged for the life of the Church and for its evangelizing mission. It is certainly not possible to ignore the foundation of many of the claims that refer to the position of women in the various social and ecclesiastical spheres. It is also necessary to recognize that the new feminine consciousness also helps men to review their mental schemes, their way of understanding themselves, of situating themselves in history and interpreting it, and of organizing social, political, economic, religious and ecclesial life.

58. It is therefore urgent to take some concrete steps, starting with opening spaces for participation for women in various sectors and at all levels, including those processes in which decisions are made, especially in matters that most directly concern them.

59. Female monastic life and the cloister of nuns deserve particular attention, due to the great esteem that the Christian community feels towards this type of life, which is a sign of the exclusive union of the Church-Bride with her deeply loved Lord. In fact, the life of the cloistered nuns, occupied mainly in prayer, in asceticism and in the fervent progress of the spiritual life, "is nothing other than a journey to the heavenly Jerusalem and an anticipation of the eschatological Church, immersed in the possession and contemplation of God." circumscribed as a place of life, the cloisters participate in the annihilation of Christ through a radical poverty that is manifested in the renunciation not only of things, but also of "space", of external contacts, of so many goods of creation. This unique way of offering the "body" introduces them in a more sensitive way to the Eucharistic mystery. They offer themselves with Jesus for the salvation of the world. Their offering, in addition to the aspect of sacrifice and atonement, takes on the dimension of thanksgiving to the Father, participating. of the thanksgiving of the beloved Son.

60. According to the traditional doctrine of the Church, consecrated life, by its nature, is neither lay nor clerical, and consequently the "lay consecration", both of men and women, is a state of profession of the evangelical counsels complete in itself. Such lay consecration, therefore, has its own value, independently of the sacred ministry, both for the person himself and for the Church.

61. Some religious institutes, which in the founder's original project were presented as fraternities, in which all members - priests and non-priests - were considered equal to each other, have acquired a diverse physiognomy over time. It is necessary for these so-called "mixed" Institutes to evaluate, through a deepening of their own founding charisma, whether it is appropriate and possible to return today to the inspiration of origin.

62. The Spirit, who at various times in history has given rise to numerous forms of consecrated life, does not cease to assist the Church, either by encouraging in existing Institutes the commitment to renewal in fidelity to the original charism, or by distributing new charismas to men and women of our time, so that they give life to institutions that respond to the challenges of the present. A sign of this divine intervention are the so-called new Foundations, with somewhat original characteristics compared to the traditional ones.

63. In some regions of the world, social changes and the decline in the number of vocations are taking their toll on consecrated life. The apostolic works of many Institutes and their very presence in certain local Churches are in danger. As has happened other times in history, there are Institutes that even run the risk of disappearing. The universal Church is extremely grateful to you for the great contribution you have made to its construction with witness and service. Today's concern does not nullify their merits or the fruits that have matured thanks to their efforts.

64. The mission of consecrated life and the vitality of the Institutes undoubtedly depend on the fidelity with which consecrated persons respond to their vocation, but they have a future to the extent that other men and women generously welcome the call of the Lord. The problem of vocations is an authentic challenge that directly challenges the Institutes, but which concerns the entire Church. Many spiritual and material energies are invested in the field of vocational ministry, although the results do not always correspond to the expectations and efforts made. It happens that, while vocations to consecrated life flourish in young Churches and in those that have suffered persecution by totalitarian regimes, they are scarce in other countries traditionally rich in vocations and missionaries.

65. The Synod Assembly has reserved special attention to the formation of those who aspire to consecrate themselves to the Lord, recognizing its decisive importance. The central objective of the formation process is the preparation of the person for the total consecration of oneself to God in the following of Christ, at the service of the mission. Saying "yes" to the call of the Lord, assuming in the first person the dynamism of vocational growth, is the inalienable responsibility of each call, which must open its entire life to the action of the Holy Spirit; It is to walk the formative path with generosity, accepting with faith the help that the Lord and the Church offer you.

66. God the Father, in the continuous gift of Christ and the Spirit, is the formator par excellence of those who consecrate themselves to Him. But in this work He uses human mediation, placing at the side of those He calls some older brothers and sisters. Formation is therefore a participation in the action of the Father who, through the Spirit, infuses the feelings of the Son into the hearts of young men and women. The trainers must be, therefore, experts in the paths that lead to God, in order to be able to accompany others on this journey. Attentive to the action of grace, they must indicate those obstacles that sometimes are not so evident, but, above all, they will show the beauty of following the Lord and the value of the charisma in which it is concretized. To the lights of spiritual wisdom they will also add those that come from human instruments that can serve as help, both in vocational discernment and in the formation of the new, authentically free man. The main training instrument is the personal discussion, which must be held regularly and with a certain frequency, and which constitutes a practice of proven and irreplaceable effectiveness.

67. Since formation must also be communal, its privileged place, for Institutes of religious life and Societies of apostolic life, is the community. In it the initiation into the fatigue and the joy of coexistence takes place. In fraternity each one learns to live with whom God has placed at their side, accepting both their positive qualities as well as their diversities and limits. Learn especially to share the gifts received for the edification of all, since "to each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common benefit" ([+[0]+]). At the same time, community life, from the first formation, must show the intrinsically missionary dimension of consecration. For this reason, in Institutes of consecrated life, it will be useful to introduce during the period of initial formation, and with the prudent accompaniment of the formator, concrete experiences that allow the exercise, in dialogue with the surrounding culture, of apostolic aptitudes, the capacity for adaptation and the spirit of initiative.

68. An explicitly formative period, which extends until perpetual profession, is also recommended for women's Institutes and for men, with regard to religious brothers. This substantially also applies to cloistered communities, which must develop an adequate program to achieve authentic formation for the contemplative life and its peculiar mission in the Church.

69. Ongoing formation, both for Institutes of apostolic life and for those of contemplative life, is an intrinsic requirement of religious consecration. The formative process, as has been said, is not reduced to the initial phase, since, due to human limitation, the consecrated person will never be able to assume that he has completed the gestation of that new man that he experiences within himself, nor of possessing in every circumstance of life the same feelings of Christ. Initial training, therefore, must be linked to ongoing training, creating in the subject the availability to allow himself to be trained every day of his life.

70. There is a youth of spirit that lasts over time and that has to do with the fact that the individual seeks and finds in each life cycle a different task to perform, a specific way of being, of serving and of loving.

71. Since the subject of formation is the person in each phase of life, the term of formation is the totality of the human being, called to seek and love God "with all the heart, with all the soul and with all the strength" ([+[0]+]) and the neighbor as oneself ([+[1]+]). Love for God and brothers is a vigorous dynamism that can constantly inspire the path of growth and fidelity.

72. In the image of Jesus, the beloved Son "whom the Father has sanctified and sent into the world" ([+[0]+]), those whom God calls to follow him are also consecrated and sent into the world to imitate his example and continue his mission. This fundamentally applies to every disciple. But it is especially valid for those who are called to follow Christ "more closely" in the characteristic form of consecrated life, making Him the "everything" of their existence. Included in your call is therefore the task of dedicating yourself totally to the mission; Furthermore, consecrated life itself, under the action of the Holy Spirit, who is the source of every vocation and every charism, becomes a mission, as the entire life of Jesus has been. The profession of evangelical counsels, by making the person totally free for the cause of the Gospel, also shows the importance it has for the mission. It must therefore be affirmed that the mission is essential for each Institute, not only in those of active apostolic life, but also in those of contemplative life.

73. Consecrated life has the prophetic mission of remembering and serving God's plan for men, as it has been announced by the Scriptures, and as is evident from a careful reading of the signs of God's providential action in history. It is the project of a saved and reconciled humanity ( [+[0]+] ). To adequately carry out this service, consecrated people must have a profound experience of God and become aware of the challenges of their own time, grasping its deep theological meaning through discernment carried out with the help of the Holy Spirit. In reality, behind the events of history there is often hidden the call of God to work according to his plans, with an active and fruitful insertion in the events of our time.

74. Everything must be done in communion and in dialogue with other ecclesial bodies. The challenges of the mission are of such magnitude that they cannot be undertaken effectively without the collaboration, both in discernment and in action, of all the members of the Church. It is difficult for isolated individuals to have a complete answer: this can normally arise from confrontation and dialogue. In particular, operational communion between the various charisms will ensure, in addition to reciprocal enrichment, a more incisive effectiveness in the mission. The experience of these years amply confirms that “dialogue is the new name for charity,” especially ecclesial charity; Dialogue helps to see problems in their real dimensions and allows them to be addressed with greater hope of success. Consecrated life, by cultivating the value of fraternal life, represents a privileged experience of dialogue. For this reason, it can contribute to creating a climate of mutual acceptance, in which the various ecclesial subjects, feeling valued for who they are, come together with greater conviction in the ecclesial communion, aimed at the great universal mission.

75. «Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. During dinner [...] he got up from the table [...] he began to wash the disciples' feet and wipe them with the towel with which he was girded » ( [+[0]+] ).

76. The specific contribution that consecrated men and women offer to evangelization is, above all, in the testimony of a life totally given to God and to one's brothers, in imitation of the Savior who, for the love of man, became a servant. In the work of salvation, in fact, everything comes from participation in the divine agape. Consecrated people make visible, in their consecration and total dedication, the loving and saving presence of Christ, the consecrated person of the Father, sent on mission. They, allowing themselves to be conquered by Him ( [+[0]+] ), prepare to become, in a certain way, an extension of their humanity. Consecrated life is eloquent proof that, the more one lives of Christ, the better one can serve Him in others, reaching the outposts of the mission and accepting the greatest risks.

77. He who loves God, Father of all, necessarily loves his fellow men, in whom he recognizes so many brothers and sisters. Precisely for this reason he cannot remain indifferent to the fact that many of them do not know the full manifestation of God's love in Christ. From here arises mainly, obeying the command of Christ, the missionary impulse ad gentes, which every conscious Christian shares with the Church, missionary by its very nature. It is an impulse felt above all by the members of the Institutes, whether they lead a contemplative or active life. Consecrated people, in fact, have the task of making Christ present, chaste, poor, obedient, praying and missionary, also among non-Christians. By virtue of their most intimate consecration to God, and remaining dynamically faithful to his charism, they cannot help but feel involved in a unique collaboration with the missionary activity of the Church. The oft-repeated wish of Therese of Lisieux, "to love you and make you love"; the ardent desire of Saint Francis Xavier: "Just as they study in literature, if they studied in the realization that God, our Lord, will demand of them, and of the talent that He has given them, many of them would move, taking means and spiritual exercises to know and feel within their souls the divine will, conforming more to it than to their own affections, saying: "Here I am, Lord, what should I do? Send me wherever you want""; as well as other similar testimonies of countless holy souls, they manifest the inalienable missionary tension that distinguishes and characterizes consecrated life.

78. "The love of Christ urges us" ([+[0]+]): the members of each Institute should repeat these words with the Apostle, since it is the task of consecrated life to work throughout the world to consolidate and spread the Kingdom of Christ, taking the announcement of the Gospel everywhere, even to the most distant regions. In fact, missionary history testifies to the great contribution they have made to the evangelization of people: from the ancient monastic Families to the most recent Foundations dedicated exclusively to the mission ad gentes, from the Institutes of active life to those of contemplative life, countless people have spent their energies on this "primary activity of the Church, essential and never concluded", since it is addressed to the growing multitude of those who do not know Christ.

79. The proclamation of Christ has permanent priority in the mission of the Church and tends to conversion, that is, to full and sincere adhesion to Christ and his Gospel. The process of inculturation and interreligious dialogue are also part of missionary activity. The challenge of inculturation must be assumed by consecrated people as a call to collaborate with grace to achieve rapprochement with diverse cultures. This requires serious personal preparation, gifts of mature discernment, faithful adherence to the indispensable criteria of doctrinal orthodoxy, authenticity and ecclesial communion. Supported by the charisma of the founders and foundresses, many consecrated people have known how to approach diverse cultures with the attitude of Jesus who "emptied himself by taking the condition of a servant" ([+[0]+]) and, with a bold and patient effort at dialogue, they have established fruitful contacts with the most diverse people, announcing to everyone the path of salvation. How many of them know how to search and are able to find in the history of people and peoples traces of the presence of God, who guides all of humanity towards discerning the signs of his redeeming will. Such a search is advantageous for consecrated people themselves: in fact, the values ​​discovered in various civilizations can encourage them to increase their commitment to contemplation and prayer, to practice community sharing and hospitality more intensely, to cultivate with greater diligence interest in the person and respect for nature.

80. Consecrated life, for its part, is in itself the bearer of evangelical values and, consequently, where it is lived authentically, it can offer an original contribution to the challenges of inculturation. Indeed, being a sign of the primacy of God and the Kingdom, consecrated life is a provocation that, in dialogue, can challenge the conscience of men. If consecrated life maintains its own prophetic force, it becomes, in the fabric of a culture, an evangelical ferment capable of purifying it and making it evolve. This is demonstrated by the history of so many saints who, in different times, have known how to live in their own time without allowing themselves to be dominated by it, pointing out new paths for their generation. The evangelical lifestyle is an important source to propose a new cultural model. How many founders, upon realizing certain demands on their time, have been able to give a response that, even with the limitations that they themselves have recognized, has become an innovative cultural proposal.

81. To adequately confront the great challenges that current history poses to the new evangelization, it is required that consecrated life allow itself to be continually challenged by the revealed Word and the signs of the times. The memory of the great evangelizers, who were once great evangelized, shows how, to face today's world, people are needed lovingly dedicated to the Lord and his Gospel. "Consecrated people, by virtue of their specific vocation, are called to manifest the unity between self-evangelization and testimony, between interior and apostolic renewal, between being and acting, highlighting that dynamism always derives from the first element of the binomial." The new evangelization, as always, will be effective if it knows how to proclaim from the rooftops what has been experienced in intimacy with the Lord. This requires solid personalities, animated by the fervor of the saints. The new evangelization demands of consecrated men and women a full awareness of the theological meaning of the challenges of our time. These challenges must be examined with careful and common discernment, to achieve a renewal of the mission. The audacity with which the Lord Jesus is announced must be accompanied by confidence in the action of Providence, which acts in the world and which "makes all things, even the failures of man, contribute to the good of the Church."

82. At the beginning of his ministry, Jesus proclaims, in the synagogue of Nazareth, that the Spirit has consecrated him to bring the Good News to the poor, to announce liberation to the captives, restore sight to the blind, give freedom to the oppressed, and preach a year of favor from the Lord ([+[0]+]). Making the Lord's mission its own, the Church announces the Gospel to all men and women, for their integral salvation. But it is directed with special attention, with a true "preferential option", to those who find themselves in a situation of greatest weakness and, therefore, of greatest need. "Poor", in the multiple dimensions of poverty, are the oppressed, the marginalized, the elderly, the sick, the little ones and those who are considered and treated as the "last" in society.

83. Following a glorious tradition, a large number of consecrated people, especially women, exercise their apostolate in the health sector according to the charism of the Institute itself. There are many consecrated people who have sacrificed their lives over the centuries in the service of victims of contagious diseases, demonstrating that dedication to the point of heroism belongs to the prophetic nature of consecrated life.

84. The Synod Fathers have highlighted the prophetic character of consecrated life, as a form of special participation in the prophetic function of Christ, communicated by the Holy Spirit to the entire People of God. It is a prophetism inherent to consecrated life as such, due to the radical following of Jesus and the consequent dedication to the mission that characterizes it. The function of sign, which the Second Vatican Council recognizes in consecrated life, is manifested in the prophetic testimony of the primacy of God and evangelical values ​​in Christian life. By virtue of this primacy, nothing can be put before personal love for Christ and for the poor in whom He lives.

85. In our world, in which the trace of God seems to have been lost, a bold prophetic testimony on the part of consecrated people is urgent. A testimony above all of the affirmation of the primacy of God and of future goods, as is evident from the following and imitation of Christ, chaste, poor and obedient, totally dedicated to the glory of the Father and the love of his brothers and sisters. Fraternal life itself is a prophetic act, in a society in which there is hidden, sometimes without realizing it, a deep longing for brotherhood without borders. Fidelity to one's own charism leads consecrated people to give a qualified testimony everywhere, with the loyalty of the prophet who is not afraid to risk even his own life.

86. In this century, as in other times in history, consecrated men and women have given witness to Christ, the Lord, by giving their own lives. There are thousands who, forced to live clandestinely by totalitarian regimes or violent groups, hindered in missionary activities, in helping the poor, in assisting the sick and marginalized, have lived and live their consecration with long and heroic sufferings, frequently coming to give their blood, in perfect conformity with the crucified Christ. The Church has already officially recognized the sanctity of some of them and honors them as martyrs of Christ, who enlighten us with their example, intercede for our fidelity and await us in glory.

87. The prophetic task of consecrated life arises from three main challenges addressed to the Church itself: they are always challenges, which contemporary society, at least in some parts of the world, launches in new and perhaps more radical forms. They directly concern the evangelical counsels of chastity, poverty and obedience, and encourage the Church and especially consecrated people to clarify and bear witness to their deep anthropological meaning. Indeed, the choice of these councils, far from being an impoverishment of authentically human values, is rather presented as a transfiguration of them. The evangelical advice should not be considered as a denial of the values ​​inherent to sexuality, the legitimate desire to dispose of material goods and to decide autonomously for oneself. These inclinations, as founded in nature, are good in themselves. The human creature, however, being weakened by original sin, runs the risk of supporting them in a disorderly manner. The profession of chastity, poverty and obedience is a warning not to underestimate the wounds caused by original sin, at the same time that, while affirming the value of created goods, it relativizes them, presenting God as absolute good. Thus, those who follow the evangelical counsels, while seeking their own sanctification, propose, so to speak, a "spiritual therapy" for humanity, since they reject the idolatry of creatures and make the living God visible in some way. Consecrated life, especially in times of difficulty, is a blessing for human life and for ecclesial life itself.

88. The first provocation comes from an Edonistic culture that demarcates sexuality from any objective moral norm, frequently reducing it to a mere game and object of consumption, compromising, with the complicity of the media, with a kind of idolatry of instinct. Its consequences are visible to all: prevarications of all kinds, which are followed by innumerable psychological and moral damages for individuals and families. The response of consecrated life consists above all in the joyful practice of perfect chastity, as a testimony of the strength of God's love in the fragility of the human condition. The consecrated person manifests that what many believe impossible is possible and truly liberating with the grace of the Lord Jesus. Yes, in Christ it is possible to love God with all your heart, putting Him above any other love, and thus love all creatures with the freedom of God! This testimony is necessary today more than ever, precisely because it is something almost incomprehensible in our world. It is a testimony that is offered to each person - to young people, to couples, to husbands and to Christian families - to show that the force of God's love can work great things precisely in the vicissitudes of human love, which tries to satisfy a growing need for interior transparency in human relationships.

89. Another provocation is today represented by a materialism eager to possess, disinterested in the demands and sufferings of the weakest and lacking any consideration for the very balance of nature's resources. The response of consecrated life is in the profession of evangelical poverty, lived in diverse ways, and frequently accompanied by an active commitment to promoting solidarity and charity.

90. In reality, even before being a service to the poor, evangelical poverty is a value in itself, in that it evokes the first of the Beatitudes in the imitation of the poor Christ. Its first meaning, in fact, consists in bearing witness to God as the true wealth of the human heart. But precisely for this reason, evangelical poverty energetically contests the idolatry of money, presenting itself as a prophetic voice in a society that, in so many areas of the world of well-being, runs the risk of losing the sense of measure and even the very meaning of things. For this reason, today more than in other times, this voice attracts the attention of those who, aware of the limited resources of our planet, advocate respect and defense of the nature created through the reduction of consumption, sobriety and a mandatory moderation of one's own appetites.

91. The third provocation comes from those conceptions of freedom that, in this fundamental human prerogative, dispense with its constitutive relationship with the truth and with the moral norm. In reality, the culture of freedom is an authentic value, closely linked to respect for the human person. But how can we not see the terrible consequences of injustice and even violence to which the deformed use of freedom leads, in the lives of individuals and peoples?

92. This testimony of consecrated persons has a particular meaning in religious life due to the community dimension that characterizes it. Fraternal life is the privileged place to discern and accept the will of God and walk together in union of spirit and heart. Obedience, enlivened by charity, unites the members of an Institute in the same testimony and in the same mission, while respecting their own individuality and the diversity of gifts. In the fraternity animated by the Spirit, each one engages with the other in a precious dialogue to discover the will of the Father, and all recognize in the one who presides the expression of the fatherhood of God and the exercise of the authority received from Him, at the service of discernment and communion.

93. One of the concerns expressed several times in the Synod has been that consecrated life be nourished by the sources of a solid and profound spirituality. It is, in fact, a priority requirement rooted in the very essence of consecrated life, since, like any baptized person but for even more pressing reasons, whoever professes the evangelical counsels is obliged to aspire with all his might to the perfection of charity. This is a commitment strongly underlined by the countless examples of holy founders and foundresses, and of so many consecrated people who have witnessed fidelity to Christ to the point of martyrdom. Aspire to holiness: this is in summary the program of all consecrated life, also in the perspective of its renewal on the threshold of the third millennium. A program that must begin by leaving everything for Christ ( [+[0]+] ), putting him before anything else in order to fully participate in his paschal mystery.

94. The Word of God is the first source of all Christian spirituality. She nurtures a personal relationship with the living God and with his saving and sanctifying will. For this reason lectio divina has been held in the highest esteem since the birth of the Institutes of consecrated life, and particularly in monasticism. Thanks to it, the Word of God comes to life, upon which it projects the light of wisdom that is the gift of the Spirit. Even though all Holy Scripture is "useful for teaching" ([+[0]+]) and "a clear and perennial source of spiritual life," the writings of the New Testament deserve particular veneration, especially the Gospels, which are "the heart of all the Scriptures." Assiduous meditation on the evangelical texts and other New Testament writings, which illustrate the words and examples of Christ and the Virgin Mary, and the apostolica vivirdi forma, will therefore be of great help to consecrated persons. Founders have constantly referred to them when accepting the vocation and discerning the charism and mission of the Institute itself.
95. The fundamental means to effectively nourish communion with the Lord is undoubtedly the sacred liturgy, especially the Eucharistic Celebration and the Liturgy of the Hours.

96. The Church has always been aware that education is an essential element of its mission. His inner Teacher is the Holy Spirit, who penetrates the most hidden depths of the heart of each man and knows the secret dynamism of history. The entire Church is animated by the Spirit and carries out its educational action with Him. Within the Church, however, consecrated persons have a specific task in this field, since they are called to introduce into the educational horizon the radical testimony of the goods of the Kingdom, proposed to every man awaiting the definitive encounter with the Lord of history. Due to their special consecration, due to the peculiar experience of the gifts of the Spirit, due to the assiduous listening to the Word and the exercise of discernment, due to the rich heritage of educational traditions accumulated over time by the Institute itself, due to the profound knowledge of spiritual truth ([+[0]+]), consecrated persons are in a position to carry out particularly effective educational action, specifically contributing to the initiatives of other educators.

97. With delicate respect, but with missionary courage, consecrated men and women demonstrate that faith in Jesus Christ illuminates the entire field of education without prejudice to human values, but rather confirms and elevates them. In this way they become witnesses and instruments of the power of the Incarnation and the force of the Spirit. This task is one of the most significant expressions of the Church that, in the image of Mary, exercises her motherhood towards all her children.

98. Institutes of consecrated life have always had a great influence on the formation and transmission of culture. This is what happened in the Middle Ages, when monasteries were the place where the cultural wealth of the past was preserved and where a new humanist and Christian culture was built. This has also been verified whenever the light of the Gospel has reached new peoples. There are many consecrated people who have promoted culture, frequently researching and defending native cultures. The Church today is very aware of the need to contribute to the promotion of culture and the dialogue between culture and faith.

99. In the same way that in the past consecrated people have known how to serve evangelization with all means, facing obstacles with genius, today they are also called again by the demand to witness to the Gospel through the media of social communication. These media have acquired a cosmic diffusion capacity through powerful technologies capable of reaching the last corner of the earth. Consecrated people, especially when they work in this field due to their institutional charisma, must acquire a serious knowledge of the language of these media, to speak about Christ effectively to modern man, interpreting their joys and hopes, their sadness and anxieties, and thus contribute to the construction of a society in which everyone feels like brothers and sisters on the path to God.

100. Christ's prayer to the Father before the Passion, so that his disciples remain in unity ( [+[0]+] ), is prolonged in the prayer and action of the Church. How can those called to consecrated life not feel involved? At the Synod, the wound of the disunity that still exists among believers in Christ was clearly perceived, and the urgency of praying and working to promote the unity of all Christians. The ecumenical sensitivity of consecrated men and women is also revived when we note that monasticism is preserved and flourishes in other Churches and Ecclesial Communities, as is the case of the Eastern Churches, or that the profession of evangelical councils is renewed, as in the Anglican Communion and in the Communities of the Reformation.

101. Sharing lectio divina in search of truth are forms of ecumenical dialogue; participation in common prayer, in which the Lord guarantees his presence ( [+[0]+] ); the dialogue in friendship and charity that makes brothers experience the sweetness of living together ( [+[1]+] ); cordial hospitality with brothers and sisters of the various Christian denominations; mutual knowledge and exchange of goods; collaboration in common initiatives of service and witness. All these forms are expressions pleasing to the common Father and signs of the will to walk together towards perfect unity along the path of truth and love. A more incisive ecumenical action will also be favored by knowledge of the history, doctrine, liturgy and the charitable and apostolic activity of other Christians.

102. Since "interreligious dialogue is part of the evangelizing mission of the Church", the Institutes of consecrated life cannot fail to commit themselves in this field, each according to its own charisma and following the indications of ecclesiastical authority. The first way to evangelize brothers and sisters of another religion will consist of the very testimony of a poor, humble and chaste life, impregnated with fraternal love towards all. At the same time, the freedom of spirit typical of consecrated life will favor the "dialogue of life", with which a fundamental model of mission and proclamation of the Gospel of Christ is carried out. To promote mutual knowledge and mutual respect and charity, religious Institutes may also cultivate appropriate forms of dialogue, in a climate of friendly cordiality and reciprocal sincerity, with the monastic environments of other religions.

103. Those who embrace consecrated life, men and women, are by the very nature of their option privileged interlocutors of that search for God, whose presence always flutters in the human heart, leading it to multiple forms of asceticism and spirituality. This search appears today with insistence in many regions, precisely as a response to cultures that tend, if not to completely deny, then to marginalize the religious dimension of existence.

104. There are many who today ask themselves in perplexity: What is the purpose of consecrated life? Why embrace this kind of life when there are so many needs in the field of charity and evangelization itself that can also be responded to without assuming the peculiar commitments of consecrated life? Doesn't consecrated life perhaps represent a kind of "waste" of human energies that would be, according to a criterion of efficiency, better used for more beneficial goods for humanity and the Church?

105. "What would the world be if it were not for the religious?" Beyond superficial assessments of functionality, consecrated life is important precisely because of its overabundance of gratuitousness and love, all the more so in a world that runs the risk of being suffocated in the confusion of the ephemeral. «Without this concrete sign, the charity that animates the Church would run the risk of cooling, the salvific paradox of the Gospel of losing its penetration, the "salt" of faith of dissolving in a world of secularization.» The life of the Church and society itself need people capable of completely giving themselves to God and others for the love of God.

106. To you, young people, I say: if you feel the call of the Lord, do not reject it! Rather enter with courage into the great currents of holiness, which distinguished men and women saints have initiated by following Christ. Cultivate the characteristic desires of your age, but respond promptly to God's plan for you if He invites you to seek holiness in the consecrated life. Admire all the works of God in the world, but fix your gaze on the realities that never perish.

107. I address you, Christian families. You, parents, thank the Lord if he has called any of your children to the consecrated life. It should be considered a great honor – as it has always been – that the Lord notices a family and chooses one of its members to invite them to follow the path of the evangelical counsels! Cultivate the desire to offer one of your children to the Lord for the growth of God's love in the world. What fruit of your marital love could you have more beautiful than this?

108. I wish to send to all men and women who want to hear my voice the invitation to seek the paths that lead to the living and true God also through the paths traced by consecrated life. Consecrated people testify that "he who follows Christ, the perfect man, also becomes more of a man." How many of them have bowed and continue to bow like good Samaritans over the countless wounds of the brothers and sisters they encounter on their path!

109. But it is above all to you, consecrated men and women, to whom at the end of this Exhortation I address my confident call: live fully your dedication to God, so that this world does not lack a ray of divine beauty that illuminates the path of human existence. Christians, immersed in the occupations and concerns of this world, but also called to holiness, need to find in you purified hearts that "see" God in faith, people docile to the action of the Holy Spirit who walk freely in fidelity to the charisma of the call and mission.
110. You not only have a glorious story to remember and tell, but a great story to build! Keep your eyes on the future, towards which the Spirit drives you to continue doing great things with you.
111. Most Holy Trinity, blessed and beatifying, make happy your sons and daughters who you have called to confess the greatness of your love, your merciful goodness and your beauty.

112. Mary, figure of the Church, Wife without wrinkle and without stain, who imitating you "virginally preserves complete faith, firm hope and sincere love", supports consecrated people in the desire to reach the eternal and only Beatitude.
